hints: Look at Fig. 4.2 from above and focus on the direction at 90 degrees to line PQ. Ball Y is moving off at an angle, so only a part of its motion counts in that sideways direction.
First find the total momentum of Y after the collision, then multiply by $\sin 27^\circ$ to pick out the perpendicular part and evaluate with correct units.
walkthrough:
**Recall what momentum component means**
You are sitting beside me, so picture line PQ as horizontal. After the hit, Y flies off upward at $27^\circ$. Its momentum $p = mv$ points along its velocity. The sideways kick is the side of the right-angled triangle opposite the $27^\circ$ angle, which is why sine appears.

**Calculate the perpendicular momentum**
First find the magnitude of momentum:
$$p_Y = m_Y v_Y = 0.25 \times 3.7$$
Then resolve perpendicular to PQ:
$$p_{\perp} = p_Y \sin 27^\circ = 0.25 \times 3.7 \times \sin 27^\circ$$
$$p_{\perp} = 0.42\text{ N s}$$
This is in $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$, which is the same as $\text{N s}$. Keep 2 s.f. to match the data.
Final answer: $p_{\perp} = 0.25 \times 3.7 \times \sin 27^\circ = 0.42\text{ N s}$ perpendicular to PQ.

hints: Before the collision both balls move only along PQ (or are at rest), so there is zero total momentum sideways. After the collision the upward sideways momentum of Y must be balanced by the downward sideways momentum of Z.
walkthrough:
**Use conservation sideways**
There is no external force sideways on the frictionless surface, so total momentum perpendicular to PQ stays at zero. That means the two sideways momenta after must cancel in size:
$$m_Z v_Z \sin 44^\circ = p_{\perp} \text{ of Y}$$
$$m_Z \times 5.5 \times \sin 44^\circ = 0.42$$
Step 2: **Solve for the unknown mass**
$$m_Z = \frac{0.42}{5.5 \times \sin 44^\circ}$$
$$m_Z = 0.11\text{ kg}$$
Y goes one way, Z goes the other way, so their magnitudes match even though directions are opposite.

hints: Think about the single interaction during contact - Z pushes on Y while Y pushes on Z at the same instant.
Recall the paired-force rule that links the sizes and directions of two forces when one object acts on another.
walkthrough:
**Apply Newton's third law**
When two bodies collide they form an action-reaction pair. The force $F_Y$ on Y by Z and the force $F_Z$ on Z by Y act for the same short time $\Delta t$ while they are in contact.

**State size and direction**
Newton's third law says paired forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction:
$$|F_Y| = |F_Z|$$
They point in opposite directions along the line of contact. No calculation is needed, this is always true even if the masses and velocities are different.
Final answer: magnitudes: equal (the same size). directions: opposite (anti-parallel).

hints: For a perfectly elastic head-on crash, the speed at which the blocks close in on each other before must equal the speed at which they move apart after. Compare the before picture with the after picture in Fig. 4.3.
walkthrough:
**Use the elastic collision speed rule**
Perfectly elastic means kinetic energy is conserved, which for straight-line collision gives a very handy shortcut: relative speed of approach = relative speed of separation.
Before, they move towards each other, so closing speed adds:
$$u_{approach} = 4 + 6 = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
Step 2: **Equate to separation speed**
After, B rebounds at $2\text{ m s}^{-1}$ one way and A moves at $v$ the other way, so they separate at $2 + v$:
$$10 = 2 + v$$
$$v = 8\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
That is the speed of A after the collision, back along its original line but in the opposite direction to its start if you track signs.
Final answer: Speed of approach $= 4 + 6 = 10\text{ m s}^{-1} =$ speed of separation $= 2 + v$, so $v = 8\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
